name: Diphenhydramine
route_note: Oral tablets, capsules or liquid; IV or IM injection; topical cream

discovery.by: George Rieveschl and Fred Huber, University of Cincinnati
discovery.note: Synthesised while searching for muscle relaxants; found to have potent antihistamine activity.

tagline: Classic sedating antihistamine used for allergy, sleep and motion sickness
summary: Diphenhydramine is one of the earliest antihistamines and remains widely sold without prescription. It relieves allergic symptoms but readily enters the brain, causing sedation, and is used as a sleep aid, an antiemetic and for drug-induced dystonia.
mechanism: Diphenhydramine is an inverse agonist at H1 receptors in the periphery and the brain. Blocking central histaminergic arousal pathways causes drowsiness.

It also blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (dry mouth, urinary retention, confusion) and, at high doses, voltage-gated sodium channels, which accounts for local-anaesthetic activity and cardiac toxicity in overdose.

history.title: Synthesis
history.detail: George Rieveschl synthesises diphenhydramine at the University of Cincinnati.

history.title: FDA approval
history.detail: Benadryl becomes the first prescription antihistamine approved by FDA.

history.title: Dimenhydrinate
history.detail: Dimenhydrinate (Dramamine), a diphenhydramine salt, is introduced for motion sickness.

history.title: Fluoxetine precursor
history.detail: Lilly chemists, starting from diphenhydramine-like structures, synthesise fluoxetine.

history.title: Online challenge warning
history.detail: FDA warns that taking high doses of diphenhydramine for social-media challenges can cause seizures, heart problems and death.

serious: Delirium and confusion in older adults
Seizures and cardiac arrhythmias in overdose

facts: Diphenhydramine is on the Beers Criteria list of medicines best avoided in older adults.
Research starting from diphenhydramine's structure led to the discovery of fluoxetine.
